newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - Dollar at 115 yen benefits Japan - OECD.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Dollar at 115 yen benefits Japan - OECD.

text.p: A dollar exchange rate of about 115 yen would benefit both Japan and its trading partners, the Deputy Secretary-General of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said on Saturday.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Kumiharu Shigehara said that, two months ago, he was concerned the yen's weakness would hurt structural reform efforts in Japan.
But those fears have been eased by the dollar's drop towards 115 yen, he added.
"I would hope that if the yen exchange rate would stabilise around that level...that would be, perhaps, useful for the Japanese and also its trading partners," he said.
With the dollar stable at 115 yen, it would also be easier for Japanese corporations to assess the advantages to domestic investments relative to advantages abroad, he added.
In addition, it would increase confidence in the household sector and would help contain Japanese exports.

The yen's fall since late 1996 has increased the price of imports, which has eliminated fears of a deflationary spiral. But there is still enough "slack" in the economy to absorb inflationary pressures, Shigehara said.
The OECD expects that slack to continue through 1997 and 1998, while Japanese growth should pick up from the third quarter of this year, he said.
"And that will probably mean that there will be little risk of inflation at this stage," he said.
He added that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) needs to pay close attention to the impact of fiscal consolidation, and other economic factors, before deciding to raise interest rates.
"The BOJ, obviously, has to watch carefully incoming indicators before they think about the stance on monetary policy," he said.
Asked whether the Fed should increase U.S. rates again, Shigehara declined to comment, but noted that a 25 basis point tightening in July would be unlikely to have much impact.
"I think the more crucial thing is how a notch increase, or no change, might affect market psychology and market expectation," he said.
